title: Patrice Lumumba
wiki_lead:
Patrice Émery Lumumba (  pə-TREESS luu-MUUM-bə; born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa; 2 July 1925 – 17 January 1961) was a Congolese politician, independence leader, and revolutionary who served as the first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic (modern day Democratic Republic of the Congo) from June until September 1960, following his party's success in the May 1960 election. Lumumba was the leader of the Congolese National Movement (MNC) from 1958 until his assassination in 1961. Ideologically an African nationalist and pan-Africanist, he played a significant role in the transformation of the Congo from a colony of Belgium into an independent republic.
Shortly after Congolese independence in June 1960, an army mutiny marked the beginning of the Congo Crisis. Both Katanga and South Kasai declared independence, which Lumumba responded to by sending the Congolese army to put down the secessions. This created a political crisis that resulted in then President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissing Lumumba and his government. This was followed by a coup led by Mobutu Sese Seko. Lumumba attempted to escape to Stanleyville to join his supporters who had established a new anti-Mobutu state called the Free Republic of the Congo, but he was captured by state authorities under Mobutu, and sent to Elisabethville in Katanga. He was tortured and later executed by the separatist Katangan authorities of Moïse Tshombe, alongside Belgian mercenaries. His body was later dissolved in acid. In 2002, Belgium formally apologised for its role in the execution, admitting "moral responsibility". In 2022, Lumumba's tooth was returned by the Belgian government to his family. 
Lumumba is widely seen as a martyr for anti-colonial liberation and the pan-African movement.

Early life and career

Patrice Lumumba was born on 2 July 1925 as Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa to Julienne Wamato Lomendja and her husband, François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer, in Onalua, in the Katakokombe region of the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo. He was a member of the Tetela ethnic group, where he was referred to with the name Élias Okit'Asombo. His original surname means "heir of the cursed" and is derived from the Tetela words okitá/okitɔ́ ('heir', 'successor') and asombó ('cursed or bewitched people who will die quickly'). He had three brothers (Charles Lokolonga, Émile Kalema, and Louis Onema Pene Lumumba) and one half-brother (Jean Tolenga). Raised in a Catholic family, he was educated at a Protestant primary school, a Catholic missionary school, and finally the government post office training school, where he passed the one-year course with distinction. He was known for being a vocal, precocious young man, regularly pointing out the errors of his teachers in front of his peers. This outspoken nature would come to define his life and career. Lumumba spoke Tetela, French, Lingala, Swahili, and Tshiluba.
Outside of his regular studies, Lumumba took an interest in the Enlightenment ideals of Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Voltaire. He was also fond of Molière and Victor Hugo. He wrote poetry, and many of his works had anti-imperialist themes. He worked as a travelling beer salesman in Léopoldville and as a postal clerk in Stanleyville for eleven years. Lumumba married three times. He married his first wife Henriette Maletaua a year after arriving in Stanleyville in 1945; they divorced in 1947. In the same year, he married Hortense Sombosia, but this relationship also fell apart and they divorced in 1951. He began an affair with Pauline Kie while still married to Hortense. While he had no children with his first two wives, his relationship with Kie resulted in a son, François Lumumba. Though he remained close with Kie until his death, Lumumba ultimately ended their affair to marry Pauline Opangu in 1951, who was 14 years old at the time.

grok_lead: Patrice Ãmery Lumumba (2 July 1925 â 17 January 1961) was a Congolese postal clerk, journalist, and politician who briefly served as the first prime minister of the independent Democratic Republic of the Congo. Born to subsistence farmers in the remote village of Onalua in the Kasai province of the Belgian Congo, Lumumba received limited formal education at a Protestant mission school before self-educating through voracious reading and advancing to clerical roles in the colonial postal service. Lumumba emerged as a vocal critic of Belgian colonial rule in the 1950s, founding the Mouvement National Congolais (MNC) in 1958 to demand immediate national independence without power-sharing federal structures that might preserve regional ethnic divisions. His party's unitary vision prevailed in the 1960 pre- independence elections, positioning him to lead the government as Belgium abruptly granted sovereignty on 30 June amid fears of prolonged unrest. Lumumba's impassioned independence day speech, decrying colonial atrocities, electrified African nationalists but alienated Belgian interests and foreshadowed conflicts over resource control in the mineral-wealthy territory. In the premiership's chaotic early months, Lumumba's decision to dismiss all Belgian officers from the Force Publique triggered widespread army mutinies, looting, and the secession of copper-rich Katanga province under MoÃ¯se Tshombe, backed by Belgian mining firms and mercenaries. Facing paralysis from these centrifugal forces and a stalled United Nations intervention, Lumumba appealed for Soviet logistical aid in August 1960, framing the crisis as neocolonial aggression but intensifying Western fears of communist encirclement in a uranium-producing state vital to nuclear deterrence. This move, amid Lumumba's centralizing impulses that disregarded Congo's ethnic fractures and institutional voids, eroded domestic support and prompted President Joseph Kasavubu to dismiss him in September. Colonel Joseph Mobutu, backed by UN forces, arrested Lumumba in efforts to stabilize the regime, but he escaped briefly before recapture and transfer to Katangese custody, where he was executed on 17 January 1961 by local forces with Belgian officers present. Declassified U.S. documents reveal President Eisenhower's authorization of CIA assassination plots against Lumumba, viewing his Soviet overtures as an existential threat, though these schemes failed while Belgian and Katangese actors completed the killing to avert a unified Congo under his influence. Lumumba's rapid demise symbolized the perils of decolonization without viable governance, cementing his legacy as a pan-African icon despite the anarchy his uncompromising nationalism unleashed.
